doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Dixieland versus rock and roll, and the band today
summary: Dixieland was the popular music when they started; rock and roll cut demand by the late fifties; the band is now at its peak, hence the Legacy CD.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well you heard me talking with Phil a little bit I think about the music that you were playing. I think it’s interesting that, perhaps from my perspective, I had sort of made this assumption that you might have been playing music that was not really what your audience would have chosen to listen to. But I’m getting the sense that I’m wrong.

This is the music that they wanted, that they liked. Remember, there was no Elvis at that time when we started and there was no rock & roll. We were the kings. This is, you go to Eddie Condon’s or you go to Nick’s and that was the epitome of jazz and of popular music. It was the best. Hot music in its finest flower. And so we had no displeasure from the audience about playing that kind of music. We got great support from them. But of © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

course by the mid to late fifties rock & roll had come in and started to stifle a demand for Dixieland. We’re fortunate there are people as old as we around that liked it at Hamilton. And we’re also fortunate, I think Hamilton is, that the younger folks, the younger bands that play more modern music or folk music, are providing that for them. We don’t want to be the sole purveyor of music. It’s great that there is a choice now between audiences.
Right. So it really is not that much different from a Hamilton band in 1965 playing current music on campus and at other colleges. That’s kind of what you were doing.

Yes except we are more proficient now. I heard you say that you noticed there’s an improvement in our band. I think we are at the peak of our powers now. That is why we made that Legacy CD. We’re not going to play any better I don’t think than that.
